title: The Gold Chain Grab on MG Road
scenario: Ramesh, while riding pillion on a motorcycle, quickly reaches out and violently snatches a gold chain from Sunita's neck as she crosses the street, immediately speeding away. Under IPC, this was charged under Section 379 (theft) or Section 392 (robbery). How is this charged under the BNS?
explanation: BNS Section 304 specifically creates a distinct statutory offence of 'Snatching' to bridge the gap between simple theft and violent robbery for street crimes.

title: Caste-Motivated Mob Attack
scenario: A group of six persons acting in concert brutally attacks and kills a man in a village solely on account of his caste and community affiliation. Under the new BNS, which provision directly penalizes this act with capital punishment or life imprisonment for every member?
options: BNS Section 103(1) general murder read with Section 3(5)
BNS Section 103(2) (Murder by group / Mob lynching on grounds of caste, race, sex, etc.)
explanation: BNS Section 103(2) is a brand-new sub-section specifically penalizing group murder / mob lynching on grounds of race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, or personal belief.

title: First-Time Shoplifting of a Book
scenario: A 19-year-old student steals a legal textbook worth ₹1,800 from a bookstore and is caught. This is his first offence, and he immediately restores the book. Under BNS Section 303(2), what unique sentencing option does the Magistrate now have that did not exist in IPC Section 379?
options: Community service upon return of the stolen property
Can only impose fine of at least ₹50,000
explanation: Under BNS Section 303(2) proviso, where stolen property value is under ₹5,000, and it is a first conviction upon return of property/value, community service may be awarded.

title: Social Media Defamation Post
scenario: An individual publishes an intentionally false and reputation-damaging allegation against a local merchant on social media. The trial court convicts him of defamation. Under BNS Section 356(2), what reformative punishment can the court now award alongside or instead of imprisonment and fine?
options: Bar from using internet for 5 years
explanation: BNS Section 356(2) replaces IPC 500 and explicitly incorporates 'community service' as an alternative punishment for defamation.

title: Doctor's Operating Room Complication
scenario: A patient dies following unforeseen complications during surgery performed by a certified surgeon. The family files a complaint of death by negligence. Under BNS Section 106(1), how is the punishment for registered medical practitioners treated compared to ordinary rash acts?
options: Doctor is immune from all criminal prosecution
Doctor's punishment is capped at 2 years, whereas ordinary death by negligence is up to 5 years
Doctor is punished under Section 103 for murder
explanation: While general death by negligence was raised from 2 to 5 years in BNS 106(1), doctors performing medical procedures are specifically capped at up to 2 years.

title: Online Financial Fraud by Phishing
scenario: Vikram creates a fake bank website and dishonestly induces Priya to transfer ₹2,50,000 to his account. In earlier days, FIRs routinely invoked IPC Section 420. Which corresponding section of the BNS should now be cited in the FIR?
explanation: IPC Section 420 (cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property) is now codified under BNS Section 318(4).

title: Matrimonial Cruelty Complaint
scenario: A woman files a complaint that her husband and mother-in-law subjected her to severe harassment over dowry demands. Under IPC, this was covered in Section 498A (offence and definition combined). Under BNS, how has this section been reorganized?
options: Split: Section 85 contains the offence/punishment, while Section 86 defines 'cruelty'
Shifted to the civil family courts exclusively
explanation: IPC Section 498A is split into two sections in BNS: Section 85 prescribes punishment (up to 3 years and fine) and Section 86 defines the dimensions of 'cruelty'.

title: Repeal of Sedition (Rajdroh)
scenario: A political activist delivers an anti-government speech criticizing official policy. Under the old IPC, police frequently registered charges under IPC Section 124A (Sedition). What is the status of 'sedition' in the BNS?
options: Retained with identical wording under Section 124
Sedition term is omitted; Section 152 penalizes acts endangering sovereignty, unity, and integrity with a higher threshold (secession/rebellion)
No offence against the state exists anymore
Sedition is now punished with only a small fine
explanation: The colonial offence of 'sedition' (rajdroh) was omitted. Section 152 of BNS targets acts endangering sovereignty, unity, or integrity of India through secession, armed rebellion, or subversive activities.

title: Syndicate Extortion and Land Grabbing
scenario: A criminal syndicate operates an extortion racket, running land-grabbing schemes and contract killings across district lines. Under IPC, prosecutors had to rely on state-specific enactments (like MCOCA) or multiple separate offences. Which new central provision in BNS tackles organized crime?
explanation: BNS Section 111 introduces a comprehensive central penal provision specifically addressing organized crime syndicates.

title: Unnatural Offences and Adult Consensual Acts
scenario: A police officer attempts to file an FIR under Section 377 for private consensual relations between two adults. The public prosecutor advises that the provision has changed. What happened to Section 377 IPC in the BNS?
options: It was renumbered as BNS Section 377 without change
It has been omitted from the BNS
The punishment was doubled to 20 years
It was moved to the Income Tax Act
explanation: IPC Section 377 has been omitted from the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, reflecting the Supreme Court's ruling in Navtej Singh Johar (2018).

title: Attempt to Murder in a Street Brawl
scenario: During a heated dispute, Karan stabs an unarmed victim in the chest with intent to kill, but timely surgical intervention saves the victim's life. What was IPC Section 307 renumbered to in the BNS?
explanation: Attempt to murder, previously the famous Section 307 IPC, is now Section 109 of the BNS.

title: Unlawful Assembly common intention vs common object
scenario: Five college students assemble outside a government office to forcibly prevent a public servant from entering. Which section defines this unlawful assembly in BNS (formerly IPC 141)?
explanation: The definition of unlawful assembly moved from IPC Section 141 to BNS Section 189(1).

title: Eve-Teasing and Indecent Gestures
scenario: A man utters sexually vulgar insults and makes obscene gestures at a woman standing at a bus stop. In IPC, this was charged under Section 509. Which section of BNS now protects the modesty of a woman against words and gestures?
explanation: IPC Section 509 is renumbered to Section 79 of BNS, positioned in Chapter V on offences against women and children.

title: Criminal Breach of Trust by Warehouse Manager
scenario: A warehouse manager entrusted with 1,000 laptops sells 200 of them on the black market for personal gain. Under IPC Section 406, the maximum imprisonment was 3 years. What is the maximum imprisonment under BNS Section 316(2)?
explanation: Under BNS Section 316(2), the maximum penalty for criminal breach of trust has been enhanced from 3 years to 5 years imprisonment.

title: Common Intention Rule Relocation
scenario: Three associates plan a bank heist and execute it together. The prosecution seeks to hold each liable for acts done in furtherance of common intention (formerly IPC Section 34). Where is this constructive liability principle located in BNS?
explanation: The common intention principle of IPC Section 34 is now codified as sub-section (5) of Section 3 in BNS.

title: Dowry Death Within Seven Years
scenario: A bride dies of burn injuries in her marital home 3 years after wedding following relentless harassment for a luxury car. Which section of BNS replaces IPC Section 304B?
explanation: IPC Section 304B has been shifted to Chapter V as Section 80 of BNS with the same 7-year statutory presumption.

title: Voyeurism via Hidden Cameras in Hotel
scenario: A hotel operator installs a hidden camera in a guest bathroom to record private acts without consent. Which BNS section replaces IPC Section 354C for voyeurism?
explanation: Voyeurism moves from IPC Section 354C to BNS Section 77 without altering penal limits.

title: Rash and Negligent Driving
scenario: A driver speeds recklessly through a busy market at 90 km/h, endangering pedestrians. In IPC, this was registered under Section 279. Which section of BNS applies?
explanation: Rash driving or riding on a public way moves from IPC Section 279 to Section 281 of BNS.
chapter: Offences Affecting Public Health, Safety, and Decency

title: Criminal Intimidation and Death Threats
scenario: An extortionist calls a businessman and threatens to shoot his children if he does not pay money within 24 hours. Under IPC, this was Section 506. Under BNS, which section penalizes criminal intimidation?
explanation: Criminal intimidation is defined in BNS Section 351(1) and punished under BNS Section 351(2).

title: Hit and Run Escape
scenario: A driver causes the death of a pedestrian through rash driving and immediately flees the scene without reporting to police or a magistrate. Under BNS Section 106(2), what is the maximum imprisonment he faces?
explanation: BNS Section 106(2) creates a dedicated aggravated hit-and-run offence carrying imprisonment up to 10 years and fine for escaping after causing death.

scenario: A foreign national located in Dubai hacks into a financial server located in Mumbai, corrupting banking records. When questioned on jurisdiction, the prosecutor invokes BNS Section 1. Does the BNS apply to this cyber offence committed outside India?
options: No, BNS only applies within India's physical land borders
Yes, Section 1(5)(c) expressly applies to any person targeting computer resources located in India
Only if the offender is an Indian citizen holding an Indian passport
No, only the Information Technology Act can apply
answer: Yes, Section 1(5)(c) expressly applies to any person targeting computer resources located in India
explanation: BNS Section 1(5)(c) explicitly extends extraterritorial jurisdiction to any person in any place without and beyond India committing any offence targeting a computer resource located in India.

scenario: In a criminal trial involving digital evidence, the defence argues that an encrypted instant message chat does not qualify as a 'document' under the penal law. How does BNS Section 2 resolve this?
options: Digital records are not considered documents under criminal law
Section 2(8) consolidates definitions and explicitly includes electronic and digital records as documents
Only paper documents with physical wax seals qualify
Only messages sent via government postal services qualify
answer: Section 2(8) consolidates definitions and explicitly includes electronic and digital records as documents
explanation: BNS Section 2(8) defines 'document' to expressly include electronic and digital records, emails, server logs, and messages stored on digital devices.

scenario: Four individuals plan a warehouse robbery. Two break open the gates while the other two stand guard outside with weapons. One guard shoots a night watchman. Where is the principle of joint constructive liability codified in BNS?
answer: BNS Section 3(5)
explanation: The principle of common intention (formerly IPC Section 34) is now codified under BNS Section 3(5), holding each participant liable for acts done in furtherance of the common intention.

scenario: A judicial magistrate convicts a first-time offender for an altercation involving minor public misconduct. Wishing to avoid sending the youth to jail, the magistrate sentences him to clean a public park for 10 hours. Under which section of BNS is this penalty recognized?
options: BNS Section 4, which adds 'Community service' as a statutory punishment
Magistrates have no power to award community service
answer: BNS Section 4, which adds 'Community service' as a statutory punishment
explanation: BNS Section 4 introduces 'Community service' as the sixth formal statutory category of punishment alongside death, imprisonment for life, imprisonment, forfeiture, and fine.

scenario: A court is calculating the fractional sentence for an attempt to commit an offence punishable with life imprisonment. Under BNS Section 6, how many years is imprisonment for life reckoned as for fraction calculations?
answer: 20 years
explanation: BNS Section 6 (formerly IPC Section 57) provides that in calculating fractions of terms of punishment, imprisonment for life shall be reckoned as equivalent to imprisonment for twenty years.

scenario: An accused is convicted of an offence carrying a maximum prison term of 4 years and fine. The magistrate sentences him to 1 year imprisonment and a fine of ₹10,000, with default imprisonment of 2 years if unpaid. Is this default sentence lawful under BNS Section 8?
options: Yes, default imprisonment can be of any length at the magistrate's discretion
No, under Section 8(3), default imprisonment cannot exceed one-fourth of the maximum term (1 year max)
Yes, provided it does not exceed 3 years
No, fine defaults can only be punished with community service
answer: No, under Section 8(3), default imprisonment cannot exceed one-fourth of the maximum term (1 year max)
explanation: Under BNS Section 8(3) (formerly IPC 65), the term of imprisonment in default of payment of fine shall not exceed one-fourth of the maximum term of imprisonment fixed for the offence.

scenario: A 6-year-old child picks up a gold coin from a neighbour's table and puts it into his pocket. The neighbour seeks to lodge a police complaint for theft under Section 303 BNS. What statutory defence applies?
options: BNS Section 20: absolute immunity under 7 years of age (doli incapax)
No defence; the child must be tried in juvenile court
answer: BNS Section 20: absolute immunity under 7 years of age (doli incapax)
explanation: BNS Section 20 (formerly IPC Section 82) provides that nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age (doli incapax).

scenario: An unconscious accident victim with severe internal bleeding is rushed to the hospital. A surgeon performs an immediate emergency laparotomy to save the victim's life without waiting for relatives' consent. Which section of BNS protects the surgeon from criminal liability?
options: BNS Section 30 (act done in good faith for person's benefit without consent in emergency)
answer: BNS Section 30 (act done in good faith for person's benefit without consent in emergency)
explanation: BNS Section 30 (formerly IPC Section 92) provides that nothing is an offence done in good faith for the benefit of a person even without consent when obtaining consent is impossible in an emergency.

scenario: At 2:00 AM, a homeowner wakes up to find an armed intruder breaking through the bedroom window carrying a sharp machete and threatening to kill anyone who moves. The homeowner shoots the intruder, causing death. Which section justifies this act?
options: BNS Section 41 (right of private defence of property against night house-breaking extends to causing death)
answer: BNS Section 41 (right of private defence of property against night house-breaking extends to causing death)
explanation: Under BNS Section 41 (formerly IPC Section 103), the right of private defence of property extends to voluntary causing of death in cases of house-breaking by night or robbery.

scenario: A cyber-criminal residing in Country X sends remote malicious code and instructions to an operative in New Delhi to hack a power grid inside India. Under IPC, prosecuting foreign abettors was procedurally complex. Which newly introduced section of BNS explicitly penalizes abetment outside India for an offence inside India?
options: BNS Section 48 (Abetment outside India for offence in India)
answer: BNS Section 48 (Abetment outside India for offence in India)
explanation: Section 48 of BNS is a newly enacted provision that explicitly criminalizes a person who, outside and beyond India, abets the commission of any act within India that would constitute an offence.

scenario: A instigates B to burn down Z's empty barn at midnight. While burning the barn, B also takes the opportunity to steal jewellery from a nearby farmhouse without A's knowledge or expectation. Is A liable for the jewellery theft as an abettor?
options: No, because under BNS Section 51 an abettor is liable for a different act only if it was a probable consequence of the abetment
Yes, an abettor is strictly liable for every single crime the perpetrator commits that night
Yes, under Section 61 for criminal conspiracy
No, because burning a barn is not an offence under BNS
answer: No, because under BNS Section 51 an abettor is liable for a different act only if it was a probable consequence of the abetment
explanation: Under BNS Section 51 (formerly IPC 111), when an act is abetted and a different act is done, the abettor is liable for the divergent act only if it was a probable consequence of the abetment.

scenario: Three persons agree in a private room to commit armed bank dacoity next month, but are arrested before taking any physical steps towards the bank. Are they guilty of criminal conspiracy, and under which section are definition and punishment now consolidated?
options: Guilty under BNS Section 61 (merging IPC 120A definition and IPC 120B punishment into one section)
Not guilty, because no overt physical act has occurred
Guilty only under BNS Section 62 for attempt
Not guilty, because an agreement alone can never constitute an offence
answer: Guilty under BNS Section 61 (merging IPC 120A definition and IPC 120B punishment into one section)
explanation: Under BNS Section 61 (consolidating IPC 120A and 120B), an agreement to commit a serious offence punishable with rigorous imprisonment of 2+ years constitutes criminal conspiracy without requiring any overt act.

scenario: A man creates a fake profile concealing his true religious identity and marital status, promises to marry a woman, engages in sexual intercourse with her, and subsequently abandons her after securing his promotion. Under the old IPC, this was litigated under rape (s. 375/90) or cheating (s. 417). Which new section of BNS specifically penalizes this conduct?
options: BNS Section 69 (Sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means or false promise of marriage)
answer: BNS Section 69 (Sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means or false promise of marriage)
explanation: BNS Section 69 is a landmark new provision explicitly criminalizing sexual intercourse by deceitful means (including false promise of employment, promotion, or marriage after concealing identity) with imprisonment up to 10 years and fine.

scenario: A 17-year-old girl is gang-raped by three men acting in furtherance of a common intention. Under BNS Section 70(2), what is the mandatory punishment prescribed for each perpetrator?
options: Imprisonment for life (remainder of natural life) and fine, or death
Imprisonment for not less than 7 years extending to 10 years
Rigorous imprisonment for 10 years and fine
answer: Imprisonment for life (remainder of natural life) and fine, or death
explanation: BNS Section 70(2) significantly expanded the minor threshold to all females under 18 years of age, prescribing imprisonment for the remainder of natural life or the death penalty for every member of the group.

scenario: An adult gang leader recruits and pays a 13-year-old child to transport illicit firearms and contraband across state checkpoints. Which newly introduced section of BNS punishes hiring or engaging a child to commit an offence?
options: BNS Section 95 (Hiring, employing or engaging a child to commit an offence)
answer: BNS Section 95 (Hiring, employing or engaging a child to commit an offence)
explanation: BNS Section 95 is a brand-new offence specifically penalizing anyone who hires, employs, or engages a child to commit crimes or in sexual exploitation/child pornography, prescribing 3 to 10 years imprisonment, fine, and liability as if the adult committed the crime personally.

scenario: Which section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 replaces IPC Section 302 for the punishment of murder?
answer: BNS Section 103(1)
explanation: BNS Section 103(1) replaces Section 302 of the IPC, prescribing death or imprisonment for life and fine for murder.

scenario: A mob of seven persons acting in concert intercepts a truck driver and lynches him to death purely on the ground of his religion and caste. Under which newly introduced statutory provision of the BNS is each member of such a group liable to capital punishment or imprisonment for life?
options: BNS Section 103(2) (Murder by a group of five or more persons on discriminatory grounds)
answer: BNS Section 103(2) (Murder by a group of five or more persons on discriminatory grounds)
explanation: BNS Section 103(2) is a historic addition specifically punishing mob lynching or group murder by five or more persons on grounds of race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, or personal belief with death or life imprisonment.

scenario: A driver speeds through an intersection, hits a pedestrian causing fatal injuries, and flees the scene immediately without reporting the incident to any police officer or magistrate. Under BNS Section 106(2), what is the maximum prison sentence for this 'hit-and-run' offence?
options: Imprisonment for a term which may extend to 10 years, and fine
Imprisonment for 2 years, or fine, or both
answer: Imprisonment for a term which may extend to 10 years, and fine
explanation: Under BNS Section 106(2), causing death by rash and negligent driving and escaping without reporting soon after the incident carries a severe penalty of imprisonment up to 10 years and fine.

scenario: An assaulted victim suffers severe body blows and is admitted to hospital under acute pain, unable to follow his ordinary pursuits for 16 days. Under the old IPC Section 320, the threshold for grievous hurt was 20 days. Does this injury qualify as grievous hurt under BNS Section 116?
options: Yes, because BNS Section 116(h) reduced the threshold of severe bodily pain or inability to follow ordinary pursuits from 20 days to 15 days
No, the threshold remains 20 days under BNS
No, hospital admission must exceed 30 days
Yes, but only if bone fracture is also proven
answer: Yes, because BNS Section 116(h) reduced the threshold of severe bodily pain or inability to follow ordinary pursuits from 20 days to 15 days
explanation: In BNS Section 116 (replacing IPC 320), the duration requirement under the eighth clause of grievous hurt was reduced from twenty days to fifteen days.

scenario: A member of an organised crime syndicate coordinates contract killings, illegal extortion networks, and cyber fraud. If a contract killing executed by the syndicate causes the death of a target, what is the mandatory punishment under newly enacted BNS Section 111(2)(a)?
options: Death or imprisonment for life, and a fine which shall not be less than ₹10,00,000
Imprisonment for 7 years and fine of ₹50,000
answer: Death or imprisonment for life, and a fine which shall not be less than ₹10,00,000
explanation: Under BNS Section 111(2)(a), if an organised crime offence results in the death of any person, the perpetrator shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and a mandatory fine of not less than ten lakh rupees.

scenario: Under old IPC Section 303, a life-convict committing murder received a mandatory death sentence, which the Supreme Court declared unconstitutional in Mithu v. State of Punjab. How has BNS Section 104 resolved this constitutional flaw?
options: By providing judicial discretion between death OR imprisonment for the remainder of natural life, along with fine
By reducing the penalty to simple imprisonment of 3 years
By exempting life convicts from new murder charges
answer: By providing judicial discretion between death OR imprisonment for the remainder of natural life, along with fine
explanation: BNS Section 104 cures the unconstitutional mandatory death sentence of IPC 303 by granting judges the discretion to award either capital punishment or imprisonment for the remainder of natural life.

scenario: An online operator uses encrypted electronic communications and foreign financial channels to knowingly incite armed secessionist activities threatening India's sovereignty. Which BNS section replaces the colonial sedition law (IPC 124A) and covers electronic/financial means?
options: BNS Section 152 (Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India)
answer: BNS Section 152 (Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India)
explanation: BNS Section 152 replaces former IPC Section 124A, specifically criminalizing acts inciting secession, armed rebellion, or subversive activities through electronic or financial means.

scenario: An insurgent leader abets an organized armed assault against military garrisons to wage war against the Government of India. Under BNS Section 147, what are the prescribed punishments?
options: Death or imprisonment for life, and fine
answer: Death or imprisonment for life, and fine
explanation: BNS Section 147 (formerly IPC 121) carries forward capital punishment or imprisonment for life and fine for waging or abetting war against the Government of India.

scenario: A mercenary group in India plans and launches an armed offensive against a friendly foreign neighbor at peace with India. In BNS Section 153, how was the colonial terminology of IPC Section 125 modernized?
options: The phrase 'Asiatic power' was replaced with 'any foreign State at peace with the Government of India'
It now applies only to Commonwealth nations
Punishment was changed to simple fine
answer: The phrase 'Asiatic power' was replaced with 'any foreign State at peace with the Government of India'
explanation: BNS Section 153 modernizes former IPC Section 125 by replacing the outdated colonial reference to 'Asiatic power' with universal 'foreign State at peace with the Government of India'.

scenario: A civilian political agitator infiltrates an army regiment and instigates soldiers to mutiny. If an armed mutiny is actually committed in consequence, what maximum sentence may the agitator face under BNS Section 160?
options: Death, or imprisonment for life, or imprisonment up to 10 years, and fine
Imprisonment up to 3 years and fine
Trial under the Army Act exclusively
answer: Death, or imprisonment for life, or imprisonment up to 10 years, and fine
explanation: Under BNS Section 160 (formerly IPC Section 132), abetment of military mutiny where mutiny is committed in consequence is punishable with death, life imprisonment, or up to 10 years and fine.

scenario: A soldier deserts his armed forces unit and flees home. His wife shelters and conceals him in their private residence knowing he is a deserter. Is the wife criminally liable under BNS Section 164?
options: No, BNS Section 164 expressly maintains an exception shielding a spouse who harbours a deserter
Yes, harbouring any military deserter carries mandatory 2 years imprisonment
Yes, under BNS Section 159 for abetting mutiny
No, but only if she reports him within 24 hours
answer: No, BNS Section 164 expressly maintains an exception shielding a spouse who harbours a deserter
explanation: BNS Section 164 (formerly IPC Section 136) contains an express statutory exception providing that the provision does not extend to the case in which the harbour is given by the spouse of the deserter.

scenario: A civilian puts on an Indian Army combat uniform and walks through a restricted zone intending onlookers to believe he is an active commissioned officer. Which section of BNS penalizes this act?
options: BNS Section 168 (Wearing garb or carrying token used by soldier, sailor or airman)
answer: BNS Section 168 (Wearing garb or carrying token used by soldier, sailor or airman)
explanation: BNS Section 168 (formerly IPC Section 140) punishes unauthorized wearing of military garb or carrying armed forces tokens with intent to deceive with imprisonment up to 3 months or fine up to ₹2,000 or both.

scenario: During an election rally, a political candidate promises that if his party is elected, the government will build a multi-specialty public hospital and waive electricity bills for poor households. Does this promise constitute electoral bribery under BNS Section 170?
options: No, the statutory exception to Section 170 explicitly excludes declarations of public policy or promises of public action
Yes, any promise of material benefit to voters constitutes bribery
Yes, punishable under BNS Section 173 with 1 year imprisonment
No, only because the election commission has not notified the code of conduct
answer: No, the statutory exception to Section 170 explicitly excludes declarations of public policy or promises of public action
explanation: Under the proviso to BNS Section 170 (formerly IPC Section 171B), a declaration of public policy or a promise of public action is not an offence of bribery.

scenario: A religious preacher tells a congregation of voters that anyone voting for Candidate X will incur divine displeasure and be excommunicated from the community. Which election offence is committed under BNS?
answer: BNS Section 171 (Undue influence at elections)
explanation: Under BNS Section 171 (formerly IPC Section 171C), inducing or attempting to induce a voter to believe they will become an object of divine displeasure constitutes undue influence.

scenario: At a polling booth, a man presents an identity card belonging to his deceased neighbor and casts a ballot in the dead man's name. Which section of BNS defines this offence of personation at elections?
answer: BNS Section 172 (Personation at elections)
explanation: BNS Section 172 (formerly IPC Section 171D) defines personation at elections as voting or applying for a ballot in the name of any other person, whether living or dead, or fictitious.

scenario: Under the old IPC, counterfeiting coins, stamps, and currency notes was scattered across Chapters XII (ss. 231-255) and XVIII (s. 489A). How has the BNS restructured this in Section 178?
options: Merged all counterfeiting offences across coins, Government stamps, and currency notes into a single umbrella section
Decriminalized counterfeiting of coins while keeping notes illegal
Transferred all counterfeiting matters to the Reserve Bank of India Act exclusively
Divided counterfeiting into four distinct new chapters
answer: Merged all counterfeiting offences across coins, Government stamps, and currency notes into a single umbrella section
explanation: BNS Section 178 unifies former IPC Sections 231, 232, 255, and 489A into a single comprehensive section punishing counterfeiting of coins, stamps, and banknotes with life imprisonment or up to 10 years and fine.

scenario: A bank teller discovers five high-quality counterfeit ₹500 notes in a bundle deposited by a merchant. To convict the merchant under BNS Section 180, what specific mental element must the prosecution establish?
options: That the person possessed the notes knowing them to be counterfeit AND intending to use them as genuine or that they may be used as genuine
Mere physical possession is a strict liability offence with no mental element required
That the person operated a printing machine personally
That the notes were imported from outside India
answer: That the person possessed the notes knowing them to be counterfeit AND intending to use them as genuine or that they may be used as genuine
explanation: Under BNS Section 180 (formerly IPC Section 489C), possession alone is not enough; the prosecution must prove knowledge of counterfeiting coupled with the intention to use as genuine.

scenario: A toy manufacturer prints novelty coupons that closely resemble Reserve Bank of India currency notes in size and colour for a board game. Under BNS Section 182, what penalty applies for making documents resembling currency notes?
options: Fine which may extend to five thousand rupees
No penalty if marked as toy money
answer: Fine which may extend to five thousand rupees
explanation: BNS Section 182 (formerly IPC Section 489E) penalizes making or using documents resembling currency notes or banknotes with a fine extending up to ₹5,000.

scenario: A group of six persons gathers outside a district collector's office carrying iron rods and stones with the declared common object of violently resisting the execution of a lawful court eviction order. What offence is constituted under BNS Section 189?
options: Unlawful assembly armed with deadly weapons under BNS Section 189(3)
No offence until violence is actually used
answer: Unlawful assembly armed with deadly weapons under BNS Section 189(3)
explanation: An assembly of five or more persons with a common object to resist the execution of any law or legal process while armed with deadly weapons constitutes an unlawful assembly under BNS Section 189(3).

scenario: During a protest, members of an unlawful assembly turn violent and start hurling petrol bombs at public buses. Under old IPC Section 148, rioting armed with a deadly weapon was punishable with up to 3 years imprisonment. What is the enhanced maximum sentence under BNS Section 191(3)?
options: Imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years, or fine, or both
answer: Imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years, or fine, or both
explanation: Under BNS Section 191(3), whoever is guilty of rioting being armed with a deadly weapon shall be punished with imprisonment up to five years, or with fine, or with both (increased from 3 years under IPC 148).

scenario: Two men get into a heated brawl inside a busy public bus station, throwing punches and causing panic among commuters, thereby disturbing the public peace. Which section of BNS penalizes this offence of affray?
answer: BNS Section 194 (Affray)
explanation: BNS Section 194 (consolidating IPC 159 and 160) punishes affray—where two or more persons disturb the public peace by fighting in a public place—with imprisonment up to 1 month or fine up to ₹1,000 or both.

scenario: A station house police officer refuses to register a First Information Report (FIR) when a woman approaches the police station to report a gang rape incident. What penal liability does the officer face under BNS Section 199?
options: Rigorous imprisonment for not less than six months extending to two years, and fine
Departmental censure only with no criminal liability
answer: Rigorous imprisonment for not less than six months extending to two years, and fine
explanation: Under BNS Section 199 (formerly IPC Section 166A), a public servant who fails to record mandatory information in relation to sexual offences faces mandatory rigorous imprisonment of 6 months to 2 years and fine.

scenario: An acid attack victim with severe facial burns is brought to a private hospital emergency room. The hospital administrator refuses to admit her without an upfront cash deposit and police clearance. Which section of BNS punishes this refusal of medical treatment?
options: BNS Section 200 (Punishment for non-treatment of victim)
answer: BNS Section 200 (Punishment for non-treatment of victim)
explanation: BNS Section 200 (formerly IPC Section 166B) punishes any hospital in-charge (public or private) who fails to provide immediate free first-aid or medical treatment to acid attack or rape victims with imprisonment up to 1 year or fine or both.

scenario: A conman wears a fake police badge, sets up an unauthorized traffic checkpoint on a highway, stops commercial trucks, and issues bogus traffic violation slips to extract money. Under which section is he prosecuted for personating a public servant?
answer: BNS Section 204 (Personating a public servant)
explanation: BNS Section 204 (formerly IPC Section 170) punishes pretending to hold office as a public servant and doing an act under colour of such office with imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both.

scenario: During a municipal anti-encroachment drive against illegal commercial shops, a shopkeeper pours kerosene over himself and attempts self-immolation to threaten and force the municipal enforcement officer to halt the demolition. Which newly introduced section of BNS explicitly penalizes this conduct?
options: BNS Section 226 (Attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power)
answer: BNS Section 226 (Attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power)
explanation: BNS Section 226 is a brand-new provision specifically criminalizing attempts to commit suicide with intent to compel or restrain any public servant from exercising lawful power, punishable with imprisonment up to 1 year, fine, or community service.

scenario: A magistrate issues and publishes a proclamation under Section 84 of the BNSS requiring an accused charged with armed robbery to appear on a fixed date. The accused intentionally absconds and fails to appear. Under which BNS section is this failure to appear penalized?
options: BNS Section 209 (Non-appearance in response to proclamation under section 84 of BNSS)
answer: BNS Section 209 (Non-appearance in response to proclamation under section 84 of BNSS)
explanation: BNS Section 209 (formerly IPC Section 174A) penalizes non-appearance in response to a proclamation published under Section 84 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 with imprisonment up to 3 years (or 7 years for proclaimed offenders).

scenario: To prevent communal clashes, a District Magistrate promulgates a curfew and assembly restriction order under law. A resident knowingly organizes a public street procession violating the order, leading to a riot. Which BNS section replaces IPC Section 188 for disobeying this promulgated order?
options: BNS Section 223 (Disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant)
answer: BNS Section 223 (Disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant)
explanation: BNS Section 223 replaces old IPC Section 188, punishing disobedience to orders promulgated by a public servant where it causes danger to human life or rioting with imprisonment up to 6 months or fine up to ₹5,000 or both.

scenario: An IT technician working for a private firm deliberately edits electronic server logs to falsely show that an executive logged into a computer from a remote city during a burglary, intending this digital record to be produced in court to mislead the trial judge. Under which section of BNS is fabricating false evidence in electronic records defined?
answer: BNS Section 228 (Fabricating false evidence)
explanation: BNS Section 228 (formerly IPC Section 192) defines fabricating false evidence, explicitly covering making false entries in electronic records or creating misleading circumstances to influence judicial proceedings.

scenario: A gang member visits the residence of an eyewitness before a trial and threatens to shoot his children unless he retracts his police statement and swears a false alibi in court. Which section of BNS specifically penalizes threatening any person to give false evidence?
options: BNS Section 232 (Threatening any person to give false evidence)
answer: BNS Section 232 (Threatening any person to give false evidence)
explanation: BNS Section 232 (formerly IPC Section 195A) specifically criminalizes threatening, intimidating, or coercing any person to give false evidence with imprisonment up to 7 years, fine, or matching punishment.

scenario: After a fatal shooting, the perpetrator's associate burns the bloodstained clothes, throws the pistol into a deep river, and formats the hotel CCTV hard drive to screen the shooter from murder charges. Which section of BNS penalizes causing disappearance of evidence?
options: BNS Section 238 (Causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen offender)
answer: BNS Section 238 (Causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen offender)
explanation: BNS Section 238 (formerly IPC Section 201) punishes causing evidence of an offence to disappear with intent to screen an offender, carrying up to 7 years imprisonment when the crime committed is capital.

scenario: An accused charged with commercial cheating is released on bail after executing a bond. He deliberately skips his trial hearings, changes his phone number, and relocates to another state without informing the court. Under BNS Section 269, upon whom does the burden of proving sufficient cause for non-appearance lie?
options: The burden of proving sufficient cause lies squarely upon the accused
The prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had no excuse
The court bailiff must prove lack of notice
The surety alone bears the burden of proof
answer: The burden of proving sufficient cause lies squarely upon the accused
explanation: Under BNS Section 269 (formerly IPC Section 229A), failure to appear in court after release on bail or bond is an independent cognizable offence where the burden of proving sufficient cause lies specifically upon the accused.
